questions.prompt: John Henry Newman's 'illative sense' (An Essay in Aid of a Grammar of Assent, ch. 9) describes how the mind reaches real, reasonable certainty on questions too rich for strict syllogistic proof alone. How does this differ from the classical demonstrative method (level 8)?
choices: Rather than one tightly linked chain of premises to a single conclusion, the illative sense weighs many converging, mutually reinforcing probabilities -- none individually a strict proof -- until their cumulative weight yields genuine, reasonable certitude, the way a judge or historian reasons from many partial clues rather than one deductive chain
The illative sense is simply another name for the exact same syllogistic method used in the classical arguments
The illative sense denies that certainty about God is possible at all
The illative sense relies purely on emotional feeling with no role for reason whatsoever
questions.correctAnswer: Rather than one tightly linked chain of premises to a single conclusion, the illative sense weighs many converging, mutually reinforcing probabilities -- none individually a strict proof -- until their cumulative weight yields genuine, reasonable certitude, the way a judge or historian reasons from many partial clues rather than one deductive chain
questions.explanation: Newman is explicit that this is still real reasoning, not a retreat into feeling -- it is simply the kind of reasoning ordinary life already uses constantly (a judge weighing circumstantial evidence, a historian weighing sources), applied to religious assent. It stands alongside, not against, the classical demonstrative method licensed in level 8.
questions.hint: Think of how a detective or a historian reasons from many partial clues, none alone conclusive, to a confident conclusion.

citations.reference: John Henry Newman, An Essay in Aid of a Grammar of Assent, ch. 9 (1870)

questions.explanation: This is the correct apologetic answer to a genuinely serious objection: converging independent evidence really can warrant more confidence than any single piece alone, which is precisely why courts weigh circumstantial evidence and historians weigh multiple sources. Cumulative-case apologetics is applying an already-trusted reasoning pattern, not inventing a special exemption for religious claims.
